How To Mount and Zero a Rifle Scope

Very good article. I think a boresighter is well worth the investment. It not only saves you time but it saves you money on wasted ammo and can be used in other ways.

Many times when you mount a scope and shoot it for the first time you may not even be hitting the paper and just getting on paper can be a challenge. Using an overly large piece of cardboard with your target in the center will help. A boresighter all but guarantees that you will be on an 8.5x11 size sheet of paper.

A boresighter can also let you know if your scope got bumped off if you drop your rifle without having to shoot it. This comes in very handy while in the middle of a hunt when shooting to check your zero may not be possible. A little pre-planning and packing your boresighter can give you the confidence that your scope is still sighted in. All you have to do is make a drawing of what the view looks like of your boresighter grid and draw a dot where your zero is located on that grid after you have initially finished sighting it in. 98% of the time it will be very close to the center of the grid. Put that piece of paper in your pack to remind you where your zero is on your boresighter if you need to double check it in the field.

You can also make a secondary zero notation for a long-range zero. For example, you sight your rifle in at 200 yards, not it on your drawing of the grid. Then you resight your scope in at a longer range like 600 yards and make a note of where that is in the boresighter. Of course, if you are using a scope with exposed target-style turrets you can do it with the turrets or if you are using a drop type reticle you can do it with the reticel but if you have a conventional hunting scope with a coin slot adjustment and plex reticle, its not that easy to know where to dial. Two zeros can come in handy depending on what caliber you are shooting and how much it drops. If you are shooting a 6.5 STW or 26 Nosler then you are probably good with one zero for most hunting. If you are shooting a short action, heavy round, having two zeros that you can confidently dial to can come in handy. You don't have to use it but its nice knowing you have it if you need it.

Something else to consider that comes up all of the time is what does Right, Left and Up, Down correlate to on your scopes adjustments. A boresighter can quickly tell you if turning your scope's adjustment in the UP direction is moving your point of impact up or your crosshairs up. Not all scopes are the same. Some will have markings other than just UP to let you know. The scope in this article reads, BULLET IMPACT UP for instance. Knowing this before you start dialing will save time and money. It really sucks when you take your first shot and see it is 6 inches low and 6 inches to the left and you make what you think are the correct adjustments and then your second shot is 12 inches low and 12 inches to the left (off the paper in the dirt).
